scene.title: A Kansas Cyclone Approaches
scene.text:
The air grows thick and dusty, and the house seems to tilt a fraction as the wind masses toward us. I hear a sharp, pounding surge from outside—the kind that makes the floorboards tremble. Uncle Henry’s voice cuts through it all, urgent and practical. He shouts to Em, “There’s a cyclone coming, Em,” and his legs carry him toward the sheds where the stock keeps its place, strong and swift as a wind-worn farmer can be. The door bang of his departure leaves a quiet edge in the room, a heartbeat of movement that rattles the teacups and my own nerves.

Then Aunt Em moves with the same sharp clarity, dropping her work in a single, practiced motion. She’s at the door in moments, eyes wide, voice tight with alarm. “Quick, Dorothy!” she cries, urgency threading through every syllable. I feel Toto tug slightly at my sleeve, and in that instant I know what’s asked of me: run for the cellar, seek shelter where the earth itself seems to hold its breath.

Toto slips from my arms as if the wind itself is tugging him away. He darts and vanishes under the bed in a blur of fur and fear, a brief, frantic pulse of dog and doorway heat and dust. I’m left standing at the doorway, Toto gone from my grasp, Aunt Em’s orders echoing in my chest as the cyclone’s approach drums a heavy rhythm on the walls. The room tightens around us, and the world tilts toward the cellar’s dark mouths and cold, earthen promises.

Choices now lie before me, shaped by a Kansas wind and a family’s need. I can feel Toto’s small, stubborn presence somewhere close, and I sense the cellar’s mouth waiting, cool and safe, beneath the floorboards and earth.

scene.title: First Whirl of the House
scene.text:
I’m standing at the doorway of our Kansas farmhouse, the air suddenly too still, as if the world is listening for something that hasn’t happened yet. Uncle Henry springs up from his chair in a snap of movement, eyes fixed on the horizon. “There’s a cyclone coming, Em,” he calls, and his voice carries with it the gravity of a man who knows what storms do to things that can’t run. He doesn’t waste a heartbeat—he’s running toward the sheds where the cows and horses are kept, as if stock and weather mend themselves with speed and purpose.

Aunt Em drops her towel and rushes to the door, the kitchen’s quiet clinging to her sleeves. She looks at the sky and back to me, and the words she doesn’t even finish sound like a command she believes with her whole heart: “Quick, Dorothy!” She tilts her head toward the cellar, her eyes sparking with a mix of fear and stubborn care. I grip Toto tighter, feeling his warmth against my chest, a tiny bright weight against the growing dark.

Toto wriggles and slips from my arms, a sudden, hopeful surprise, and—before I can catch him again—he darts toward the bed. He’s beneath the shabby frame in a heartbeat, tiny paws scrabbling for a hiding place, and I’m left with the doorway’s cold air on my skin and the storm-wind’s distant roar rising outside.

The house trembles a little, the wind threading through the cracks like a living thing. I stand there, Toto gone under the bed, Aunt Em barking out orders, Uncle Henry already a shadow sprinting toward the sheds. The cyclone’s approach feels almost like a promise—not just to the roof, but to all the world we know, tilting it off its hinges and asking us to choose what comes next.

scene.title: Warning and Flight
scene.text:
The farmhouse kitchen shakes with the unseen threat outside as Uncle Henry suddenly rises from his chair. He points toward the barn and the sheds beyond, voice tight with urgency: there’s a cyclone coming, Em. Then he doesn’t hesitate—he darts for the stock sheds, calling to me to stay safe and keep Toto close as he rushes away to safeguard the animals.

Aunt Em bursts from her chores at the sink, hands still wet with dishwater, and comes to the door in a whirl of movement and worry. One look at the sky, at the horizon skimming with dark cloud, is all she needs to know. She drops her towel and the washing, and with a sharp edge to her voice orders me: Quick, Dorothy! Run for the cellar!

Toto, restless as ever, wriggles free from my grip mid-step. He darts toward the closest shelter, a frantic little blur, and then—suddenly—he leaps from my arms and dives beneath the bed, vanishing into the shadowed space where dust motes drift like small ghosts.

The room tilts with the wind’s distant howl, and I stand at the doorway with Toto’s absence and Aunt Em’s shouted orders echoing in my ears, feeling very small but very determined. The cellar looms below, a promise of safety if we can reach it through the fear and the wind-smarting cold.

scene.title: Cyclone's Threshold
scene.text:
Dust from the prairie swirls in a widening channel along the doorway as the house groans with the wind’s sudden impatience. Uncle Henry’s voice cuts through the clamor before I even spot the danger: there’s a cyclone coming, Em, and he dashes toward the sheds to look after the stock. The world tilts a little, and for a breath I grip Toto tighter, half-expecting him to shrink away with fear like I’m the one who’ll make things worse.

Aunt Em’s hands pause on her wet dishes, then she drops her work and rushes to the door. Her eyes meet mine, urgent and ancient as the land itself. “Quick, Dorothy!” she commands, voice firm as the rails on the fence. “Run for the cellar!” The words come hot and fast, and I feel the weight of Toto’s small body tug as I lift him higher, toward the safety she promises with that steady, practical tone she always wears when trouble presses in.

Then Toto—my constant, brave little troublemaker—lets go of my arms. He slips from my grasp and darts under the bed, small and quick as a shadow. The room settles into a tense hush, and I know we’re not safe yet, but we’re not yet conquered either.

After Toto disappears under the bed, I cross the room, kneel beside it, and reach beneath it to retrieve him.
